subtopic: Anthropometry — body composition, somatotypes, growth & maturation
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, which limitation makes BMI an incomplete description of an athlete's physique?
options: It accounts for muscularity in athletes
It directly estimates body-fat percentage
It does not separate fat mass from lean mass
It identifies regional fat distribution
explanation: BMI uses height and mass but cannot separate adipose tissue from lean tissue or describe its distribution.

subtopic: Anthropometry — body composition, somatotypes, growth & maturation
text: A 102-kg rugby forward is labelled 'overweight' by BMI, but his skinfolds are low. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: BMI directly measures adiposity
BMI cannot distinguish muscle from fat
BMI is valid only in endurance athletes
BMI identifies regional fat pattern
explanation: BMI uses height and mass but cannot distinguish muscular lean tissue from adipose tissue.

subtopic: Anthropometry — body composition, somatotypes, growth & maturation
text: A gymnast's BMI falls after a diet, but waist circumference and performance are unchanged. What does BMI alone fail to show?
options: Whether lost mass was fat or lean tissue
The athlete’s biological maturation
The athlete’s regional fat distribution
Whether the athlete trains aerobically
explanation: A change in BMI does not identify which tissue compartment changed.

subtopic: Anthropometry — body composition, somatotypes, growth & maturation
text: Two rowers have the same BMI but different skinfold profiles. What is the soundest next step before comparing their physique?
options: Assign both athletes the same somatotype
Assume identical body composition from BMI
Diagnose excess adiposity from BMI alone
Use a validated body-composition assessment
explanation: BMI is a screening ratio; a more appropriate body-composition method is needed for a meaningful comparison.

subtopic: Anthropometry — body composition, somatotypes, growth & maturation
text: A coach asks whether a muscular sprinter with a BMI of 27 is obese. Which response is most defensible?
options: A BMI above 25 proves high body fat
Interpret BMI with body-composition context
BMI is irrelevant for every athlete
BMI alone determines readiness for competition
explanation: Muscularity can elevate BMI without indicating the athlete’s fat mass; interpretation requires context.

subtopic: Anthropometry — body composition, somatotypes, growth & maturation
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, which method is based most directly on measuring subcutaneous fat thickness at standardized sites?
options: Skinfold assessment
Air-displacement plethysmography
Bioelectrical impedance analysis
Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry
explanation: Skinfold calipers estimate subcutaneous adiposity from the thickness of standardized skinfold sites.

subtopic: Anthropometry — body composition, somatotypes, growth & maturation
text: A volleyball squad is being monitored over eight weeks. Which field measure samples subcutaneous adiposity at specified anatomical sites?
options: Bioelectrical impedance with hydration control
Skinfolds at standardized sites
Air-displacement plethysmography
Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry
explanation: Skinfold assessment estimates subcutaneous fat from standardized skinfold sites.

subtopic: Anthropometry — body composition, somatotypes, growth & maturation
text: A hydrated athlete has unstable bioelectrical-impedance readings. Which method directly measures the thickness of a lifted skinfold?
options: Waist-to-height ratio
Hydrostatic weighing
Skinfold assessment
Air-displacement plethysmography
explanation: Calipers measure the thickness of a standardized fold of subcutaneous tissue.

subtopic: Anthropometry — body composition, somatotypes, growth & maturation
text: A rural training centre has no DXA or BodPod, but a trained assessor and calibrated calipers are available. Which method is most feasible for serial field monitoring?
options: Skinfold assessment
Magnetic-resonance imaging
Air-displacement plethysmography
Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry
explanation: A trained assessor can use standardized skinfold sites for practical serial monitoring in the field.

subtopic: Anthropometry — body composition, somatotypes, growth & maturation
text: To improve repeatability when tracking an athlete's skinfolds, which practice is most important?
options: Measure only after heavy exercise sessions
Measure different sites at each visit
Use identical sites and technique each visit
Replace skinfolds with BMI alone
explanation: Standardized sites and technique reduce measurement error in repeated skinfold assessments.

subtopic: Anthropometry — body composition, somatotypes, growth & maturation
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, in Heath-Carter somatotyping, mesomorphy primarily represents relative:
options: Linearity and slenderness
Muscular development
Biological maturation
Subcutaneous adiposity
explanation: Mesomorphy describes relative musculoskeletal development, whereas endomorphy describes adiposity and ectomorphy linearity.

subtopic: Anthropometry — body composition, somatotypes, growth & maturation
text: A wrestler has broad limbs and marked muscular development relative to his frame. Which Heath-Carter component best captures that feature?
options: Chronological age
Ectomorphy
Endomorphy
Mesomorphy
explanation: Mesomorphy represents relative musculoskeletal development.

subtopic: Anthropometry — body composition, somatotypes, growth & maturation
text: When describing the muscular component of a swimmer's somatotype, which term should be used?
options: Mesomorphy
Endomorphy
Maturity offset
Ectomorphy
explanation: In Heath-Carter somatotyping, mesomorphy denotes relative muscular and skeletal development.

subtopic: Anthropometry — body composition, somatotypes, growth & maturation
text: An athlete's longitudinal profile shows a higher mesomorphy rating after resistance training. What does that rating primarily describe?
options: The distribution of subcutaneous fat
The timing of peak height velocity
Relative muscular development
The athlete’s training motivation
explanation: Mesomorphy is the somatotype component concerned with relative muscular development.

subtopic: Anthropometry — body composition, somatotypes, growth & maturation
text: A coach wants to separate the muscular and linear features of a lean basketball player. Which statement is correct?
options: Mesomorphy indicates competition anxiety
Mesomorphy measures chronological age
Mesomorphy estimates regional adiposity
Mesomorphy describes muscular development
explanation: Mesomorphy refers to muscular development; ectomorphy describes relative linearity.

subtopic: Anthropometry — body composition, somatotypes, growth & maturation
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, why should biological maturation be considered when comparing adolescent strength results?
options: It has no relationship to adolescent body size
It affects size, strength, and adaptation timing
Its timing is identical among athletes of the same age
Chronological age precisely identifies maturation status
explanation: Growth and maturation influence body size and neuromuscular capacity, so chronological-age comparisons can mislead.

subtopic: Anthropometry — body composition, somatotypes, growth & maturation
text: Two 15-year-old sprinters have the same chronological age but are at different stages of peak height velocity. Why should strength results be interpreted cautiously?
options: Maturation affects flexibility only
Chronological age removes maturation effects
Maturation alters size, strength, and timing
Adolescent strength testing is always invalid
explanation: Biological maturation influences body size, strength expression, and the timing of training adaptations.

subtopic: Anthropometry — body composition, somatotypes, growth & maturation
text: An early-maturing footballer is temporarily much larger than teammates. What is the fairest selection approach?
options: Consider maturity status with performance data
Select mainly on current body size and strength
Ignore maturation when comparing athletes
Compare athletes only by chronological age
explanation: Maturity status can create temporary size and strength advantages, so it should be considered with performance and development.

subtopic: Anthropometry — body composition, somatotypes, growth & maturation
text: During a rapid growth spurt, why might a youth athlete need closer monitoring of training response?
options: Growth eliminates injury risk during training
Growth guarantees identical adaptation in every athlete
Growth changes only the athlete’s motivation
Growth can alter coordination and tissue tolerance
explanation: Rapid growth can change coordination and mechanical loading while tissue tolerance adapts at a different rate.

subtopic: Exercise Physiology — energy systems, fatigue, adaptation
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, which energy system supplies the highest immediate power during a maximal effort lasting only a few seconds?
options: Oxidative phosphorylation
Beta oxidation
The phosphagen system
Gluconeogenesis
explanation: Stored ATP and phosphocreatine provide rapid ATP resynthesis for very brief, high-power efforts.

subtopic: Exercise Physiology — energy systems, fatigue, adaptation
text: A sprinter's block-start effort lasts about three seconds. Which energy system supplies the greatest immediate power?
options: Fat oxidation during prolonged exercise
Aerobic oxidation over the whole effort
Anaerobic glycolysis after several seconds
The phosphagen system in the first seconds
explanation: The phosphagen system provides very high power for the first seconds of maximal effort.

subtopic: Exercise Physiology — energy systems, fatigue, adaptation
text: During a single maximal lift lasting less than five seconds, which system is the primary immediate ATP source?
options: The phosphagen system
The oxidative system
Aerobic fat metabolism
Lactate clearance
explanation: Stored ATP and phosphocreatine support the highest immediate power during a brief maximal effort.

subtopic: Exercise Physiology — energy systems, fatigue, adaptation
text: A shot-putter produces force during a single explosive release. Which energy contribution is dominant during that brief action?
options: Oxidative phosphorylation
The phosphagen system
Fatty-acid oxidation
Gluconeogenesis
explanation: The brief explosive action relies predominantly on stored ATP and phosphocreatine.

subtopic: Exercise Physiology — energy systems, fatigue, adaptation
text: In the opening seconds of a maximal cycling sprint, which pathway has the highest power contribution?
options: Beta-oxidation
Aerobic metabolism
The phosphagen system
Glycolysis alone
explanation: The phosphagen pathway has the greatest immediate power capacity at the start of a maximal sprint.

subtopic: Exercise Physiology — energy systems, fatigue, adaptation
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, which adaptation most directly improves sustained aerobic ATP production?
options: Lower stroke volume during exercise
Reduced oxygen extraction by muscle
Reduced capillary density in muscle
Greater mitochondrial oxidative capacity
explanation: Endurance training can increase mitochondrial capacity and the ability to produce ATP oxidatively.

subtopic: Exercise Physiology — energy systems, fatigue, adaptation
text: After several weeks of aerobic training, an endurance athlete can hold the same pace with less metabolic strain. Which adaptation most directly supports this?
options: Greater mitochondrial oxidative capacity
Greater resting glycogen depletion after training
Reduced capillary supply to active muscle
Lower oxygen extraction by working muscle
explanation: More capable mitochondria support sustained oxidative ATP production at a given workload.

subtopic: Exercise Physiology — energy systems, fatigue, adaptation
text: Which muscle change would most directly improve an athlete’s ability to produce ATP aerobically during a long event?
options: Reduced oxidative enzyme activity
Greater mitochondrial oxidative capacity
Lower muscle blood flow during exercise
A smaller capillary network in muscle
explanation: Mitochondrial oxidative capacity is central to sustained aerobic ATP production.

subtopic: Exercise Physiology — energy systems, fatigue, adaptation
text: A cyclist recovers more quickly between submaximal intervals after endurance training. Which adaptation is most relevant?
options: A shift away from aerobic oxygen use
Reduced mitochondrial enzyme activity
Greater mitochondrial oxidative capacity
Lower oxygen extraction during exercise
explanation: Improved oxidative machinery helps regenerate ATP and process metabolites during and between aerobic efforts.

subtopic: Exercise Physiology — energy systems, fatigue, adaptation
text: At the same submaximal workload, an endurance-trained runner shows lower lactate and better recovery. Which adaptation is a likely contributor?
options: Greater mitochondrial oxidative capacity
Reduced oxidative capacity after training
Lower oxygen delivery to active muscle
Reduced aerobic enzyme activity in muscle
explanation: Enhanced oxidative capacity can support aerobic ATP production and reduce reliance on rapid glycolysis at a fixed workload.

subtopic: Exercise Physiology — energy systems, fatigue, adaptation
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, the Fick principle expresses oxygen consumption as cardiac output multiplied by the:
options: Blood lactate concentration
Ventilatory equivalent
Respiratory exchange ratio
Arterial-venous oxygen difference
explanation: VO2 equals cardiac output multiplied by the difference between arterial and venous oxygen content.

subtopic: Exercise Physiology — energy systems, fatigue, adaptation
text: A cyclist's cardiac output is unchanged, but oxygen consumption rises during a training comparison. Which Fick-principle term must have increased?
options: Resting respiratory rate
Arterial-venous oxygen difference
Venous carbon-dioxide pressure
Blood glucose concentration
explanation: The Fick principle states that VO2 equals cardiac output multiplied by the arterial-venous oxygen difference.

subtopic: Exercise Physiology — energy systems, fatigue, adaptation
text: During testing, cardiac output is 20 L/min and oxygen consumption is 4 L/min. What is the arterial-venous oxygen difference?
options: 0.20 L O2/L blood
0.05 L O2/L blood
0.10 L O2/L blood
0.80 L O2/L blood
explanation: By the Fick equation, 4 divided by 20 equals an arterial-venous oxygen difference of 0.20 L O2 per litre of blood.

subtopic: Exercise Physiology — energy systems, fatigue, adaptation
text: A trained athlete extracts more oxygen per litre of blood at the exercising muscle. Which Fick-principle variable best represents this peripheral adaptation?
options: Pulmonary ventilation during exercise
Cardiac output as the central pump variable
Stroke volume as the only variable
Arterial-venous oxygen extraction difference
explanation: The arterial-venous oxygen difference reflects the amount of oxygen removed from each litre of blood by the tissues.

subtopic: Exercise Physiology — energy systems, fatigue, adaptation
text: A test records cardiac output of 18 L/min and an arterial-venous oxygen difference of 0.25 L O2/L blood. What is the calculated oxygen consumption?
options: 0.72 L/min
4.50 L/min
18.25 L/min
72.00 L/min
explanation: Multiplying 18 L/min by 0.25 L O2/L blood gives 4.50 L O2/min.

subtopic: Exercise Physiology — energy systems, fatigue, adaptation
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, during repeated sprints, phosphocreatine resynthesis between efforts depends substantially on:
options: Oxidative metabolism during adequate recovery
A fixed rate despite recovery duration
Glycogen depletion during repeated efforts
Passive stretching between sprint efforts
explanation: Phosphocreatine resynthesis is largely oxidative and is improved when recovery permits oxygen-supported metabolism.

subtopic: Exercise Physiology — energy systems, fatigue, adaptation
text: After a 20-second sprint, an athlete receives a low-intensity recovery before repeating the effort. What best supports phosphocreatine restoration?
options: Fat oxidation only during the sprint
Complete muscle inactivity without oxygen delivery
Immediate depletion of muscle glycogen
Oxidative metabolism during adequate recovery
explanation: Phosphocreatine resynthesis during recovery depends substantially on oxidative metabolism and oxygen availability.

subtopic: Exercise Physiology — energy systems, fatigue, adaptation
text: When recovery between maximal sprints is shortened from three minutes to 20 seconds, why may the next sprint power fall?
options: The athlete cannot resynthesize ATP between efforts
Glycogen stores are instantly depleted during recovery
Oxidative recovery has not restored phosphocreatine
Lactate is the only fuel for the next sprint
explanation: Short recovery may not allow oxidative phosphocreatine resynthesis to approach the pre-sprint level.

subtopic: Exercise Physiology — energy systems, fatigue, adaptation
text: A team wants to preserve repeated-sprint power during a congested session. Which recovery choice is most defensible?
options: Remove recovery between all sprints
Allow adequate recovery for PCr resynthesis
Use passive stretching between efforts
Replace recovery with another maximal sprint
explanation: Adequate recovery provides time and oxygen for oxidative phosphocreatine resynthesis.

subtopic: Physiotherapy — injury mechanisms, basic rehabilitation principles
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, functional ankle instability after a sprain is most closely associated with deficits in:
options: Mechanical laxity without sensorimotor loss
Plantar-flexor weakness as the only deficit
Proprioception and neuromuscular control
Isolated knee proprioception loss
explanation: Functional instability can persist through impaired sensorimotor control even when structural laxity is limited.

subtopic: Physiotherapy — injury mechanisms, basic rehabilitation principles
text: A footballer reports repeated giving-way on uneven ground months after an ankle sprain. Which deficit is most likely contributing?
options: Cardiorespiratory endurance alone during running
Upper-limb flexibility alone in the athlete
Bone mineral density alone after a sprain
Proprioception and neuromuscular control
explanation: Functional ankle instability commonly involves impaired proprioception and neuromuscular control after injury.

subtopic: Physiotherapy — injury mechanisms, basic rehabilitation principles
text: A rehabilitation plan for recurrent ankle sprain includes single-leg balance and perturbation drills. Which impairment is it primarily targeting?
options: Proprioception and neuromuscular control
Reduced lung volume during exercise
Loss of muscle glycogen during rest
Excess body fat as the primary deficit
explanation: Balance and perturbation work challenges sensorimotor control and proprioceptive responses around the ankle.

subtopic: Physiotherapy — injury mechanisms, basic rehabilitation principles
text: An ankle ligament has healed, but the athlete still feels unstable during a cut. Which finding best explains the functional problem?
options: A fracture confirmed on imaging as the cause
Persistent proprioceptive and neuromuscular deficits
Improved joint-position sense after complete healing
Increased aerobic capacity after rehabilitation
explanation: Mechanical healing does not automatically restore sensorimotor control required for dynamic stability.

subtopic: Physiotherapy — injury mechanisms, basic rehabilitation principles
text: During single-leg landing, an athlete cannot correct ankle position after a small perturbation. Which rehabilitation target is most appropriate?
options: Resting heart rate and blood pressure
Visual acuity during the landing task
Proprioception and neuromuscular control
Body-mass index without movement testing
explanation: The delayed correction suggests impaired proprioceptive input and neuromuscular response.

subtopic: Physiotherapy — injury mechanisms, basic rehabilitation principles
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, a non-contact pivot injury with a pop, immediate swelling, and instability most strongly suggests injury to the:
options: Posterior cruciate ligament
Meniscal injury
Patellar tendon injury
Anterior cruciate ligament
explanation: The mechanism and early swelling pattern are characteristic of an acute ACL injury.

subtopic: Physiotherapy — injury mechanisms, basic rehabilitation principles
text: A footballer plants and pivots with valgus collapse, hears a pop, and develops rapid knee swelling. Which structure is most suspicious?
options: Anterior cruciate ligament injury
Medial meniscal injury during the pivot
Achilles tendon injury during running
Deltoid ligament injury at the ankle
explanation: A non-contact pivot, pop, immediate swelling, and instability are classic concerns for ACL injury.

subtopic: Physiotherapy — injury mechanisms, basic rehabilitation principles
text: A skier twists the knee while the boot remains fixed, followed by a pop and haemarthrosis. Which injury should be prioritized clinically?
options: Isolated calf muscle strain after sprinting
Anterior cruciate ligament injury
Distal radius fracture after a fall
Lateral elbow sprain after contact
explanation: A fixed-foot twisting mechanism with a pop and early haemarthrosis raises strong concern for ACL injury.

subtopic: Physiotherapy — injury mechanisms, basic rehabilitation principles
text: An athlete has a positive Lachman test and instability after a non-contact deceleration. Which ligament is most likely involved?
options: Posterior cruciate ligament
Medial collateral ligament
Anterior cruciate ligament
Patellar ligament
explanation: The Lachman test primarily assesses anterior translation related to ACL integrity.

subtopic: Physiotherapy — injury mechanisms, basic rehabilitation principles
text: After a sudden change of direction, a player reports a pop, immediate swelling, and difficulty trusting the knee. Which diagnosis warrants urgent assessment?
options: An anterior cruciate ligament injury
Delayed-onset muscle soreness after training
A simple finger sprain after contact
An uncomplicated skin abrasion
explanation: This mechanism and acute presentation warrant assessment for ACL injury and associated internal derangement.

subtopic: Physiotherapy — injury mechanisms, basic rehabilitation principles
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, which rehabilitation progression is most defensible after an uncomplicated sports injury?
options: Rely on passive treatment without active loading
Return directly from daily activity to competition
Use a fixed calendar regardless of function
Progress from symptoms to sport-specific loading
explanation: Criteria-based progression restores capacity while monitoring symptoms, recovery, and movement quality.

subtopic: Physiotherapy — injury mechanisms, basic rehabilitation principles
text: An athlete can walk pain-free after an ankle sprain but develops pain during a single-leg hop. What is the next rehabilitation principle?
options: Return directly to unrestricted competition
Avoid loading until the season ends
Progress loading using symptoms and function
Use analgesia as the only clearance criterion
explanation: Rehabilitation should progress from tolerated function toward sport-specific loading rather than relying on walking alone.

subtopic: Physiotherapy — injury mechanisms, basic rehabilitation principles
text: During hamstring rehabilitation, an athlete tolerates jogging but not maximal sprinting. Which progression is most appropriate?
options: Advance from controlled to sport-specific loading
Return immediately to maximal competition
Stop all strengthening permanently during rehabilitation
Test resting range of motion only before clearance
explanation: Hamstring rehabilitation should progress gradually from controlled loading to running and sprint demands as tolerated.

subtopic: Physiotherapy — injury mechanisms, basic rehabilitation principles
text: A tendinopathy patient has stable symptoms with slow resistance exercise. Which next step is most defensible?
options: Replace exercise with complete bed rest throughout recovery
Clear the athlete because resting pain is absent
Add maximal jumping without preparation or progression
Increase sport-specific load while monitoring symptoms
explanation: Progressive, symptom-monitored loading helps bridge from therapeutic exercise to sport demands.

subtopic: Physiotherapy — injury mechanisms, basic rehabilitation principles
text: After six weeks of immobilization, an athlete has regained basic walking but not cutting ability. Which rehabilitation sequence is sound?
options: Begin full-speed cutting before strength work
Restore mobility and strength before sport drills
Use imaging as the only return-to-sport test
Avoid loaded movement until competition day
explanation: A graded sequence restores foundational capacity before exposing the athlete to complex sport-specific loads.

subtopic: Physiotherapy — injury mechanisms, basic rehabilitation principles
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, a return-to-play decision should integrate symptoms, function, sport demands, and:
options: Risk-informed clinical and multidisciplinary criteria
Injury date combined with a fixed time-based schedule
Pain report combined with functional testing alone
A performance test without considering sport context
explanation: Time is only one factor; readiness requires functional, medical, sport-demand, and risk information.

subtopic: Physiotherapy — injury mechanisms, basic rehabilitation principles
text: An athlete's knee symptoms have settled, but repeated cutting still produces apprehension. What should a return-to-play decision integrate?
options: Use only the athlete’s desire and motivation to compete
Use one resting pain score without function testing
Use only elapsed days since the injury occurred
Integrate symptoms, function, sport demands, and risk
explanation: Return-to-play decisions should combine symptoms, functional capacity, sport demands, and clinical risk assessment.

subtopic: Physiotherapy — injury mechanisms, basic rehabilitation principles
text: A midfielder has full quadriceps strength after injury but has not tolerated high-speed direction changes. What is missing from the clearance decision?
options: A normal resting pulse as the only clearance measure
The athlete’s jersey number as the only identifier
Sport demands and multidisciplinary risk assessment
A longer period of complete inactivity before testing
explanation: Strength alone does not reproduce the speed, cutting, and decision demands of the sport; clearance should be risk-informed and multidisciplinary.

subtopic: Physiotherapy — injury mechanisms, basic rehabilitation principles
text: An athlete requests selection while still reporting swelling after training. Which response is most defensible?
options: Clear participation because motivation is strong
Reassess symptoms, function, sport demands, and risk
Ignore sport demands if strength is clinically normal
Use the calendar date as the only clearance criterion
explanation: Persistent symptoms require reassessment against functional and sport-specific criteria before return.

subtopic: Biomechanics — movement analysis, force, kinematics
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, joint torque is calculated most directly as force multiplied by the perpendicular:
options: Angular velocity
Linear impulse
Moment arm
Segment mass
explanation: Torque is the rotational effect of force and equals force multiplied by its perpendicular moment arm.

subtopic: Biomechanics — movement analysis, force, kinematics
text: A force of 150 N acts perpendicular to a 0.40-m moment arm at the knee. What torque does it create?
options: 15 N·m
60 N·m
explanation: Torque equals force multiplied by perpendicular moment arm: 150 N multiplied by 0.40 m equals 60 N·m.

subtopic: Biomechanics — movement analysis, force, kinematics
text: If the same external force acts with twice the perpendicular moment arm, what happens to the joint torque?
options: It is halved
It doubles
It remains unchanged
It becomes zero
explanation: With force unchanged, doubling the perpendicular moment arm doubles torque.

subtopic: Biomechanics — movement analysis, force, kinematics
text: For a fixed force magnitude, when is the turning effect about a joint greatest?
options: When force passes through the centre of the joint
When force is parallel to the moment arm
When force acts at about 90° to the lever arm
When the moment arm is zero at the joint
explanation: Torque equals force multiplied by the perpendicular moment arm; for a fixed force, the turning effect is greatest when the force's line of action is approximately perpendicular to the lever arm.

subtopic: Biomechanics — movement analysis, force, kinematics
text: A 80-N force is applied 0.25 m perpendicular to a handle's pivot. What torque is produced?
options: 20 N·m
80 N·m
explanation: Torque equals 80 N multiplied by 0.25 m, giving 20 N·m.

subtopic: Biomechanics — movement analysis, force, kinematics
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, reducing braking impulse during sprint ground contact primarily reduces:
options: Vertical impulse during that contact
Propulsive impulse in the next contact
Angular displacement of the trunk
Horizontal deceleration of the body
explanation: Braking impulse is the horizontal impulse that slows the body during ground contact.

subtopic: Biomechanics — movement analysis, force, kinematics
text: A sprinter's foot lands far in front of the centre of mass. Reducing the resulting braking impulse primarily reduces:
options: Vertical body-mass change
Horizontal deceleration of the body
Arm-swing frequency during contact
Oxygen-carrying capacity of blood
explanation: A negative horizontal impulse changes horizontal momentum and contributes to deceleration.

subtopic: Biomechanics — movement analysis, force, kinematics
text: Force-plate data show a smaller negative horizontal impulse during ground contact. What mechanical outcome is expected?
options: More horizontal speed is lost
Vertical mass disappears
Less horizontal deceleration occurs
The athlete’s limb length changes
explanation: A smaller negative impulse produces a smaller reduction in horizontal velocity.

subtopic: Biomechanics — movement analysis, force, kinematics
text: A coach cues a sprinter to place the foot closer beneath the centre of mass. Which immediate mechanical aim is most relevant?
options: Increase passive body mass during ground contact
Decrease the athlete’s effective leg length
Eliminate all vertical ground force during contact
Reduce braking impulse and speed loss
explanation: Foot placement nearer the centre of mass can reduce the braking impulse during early ground contact.

subtopic: Biomechanics — movement analysis, force, kinematics
text: Two athletes enter ground contact at the same speed, but one produces a lower negative horizontal impulse. Which result is most likely?
options: A greater loss of forward velocity
Less horizontal deceleration
No change in horizontal momentum
A higher resting metabolic rate
explanation: Lower negative impulse means a smaller reduction in forward horizontal momentum.

subtopic: Biomechanics — movement analysis, force, kinematics
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, the vertical ground-reaction force during running is measured most directly with a:
options: Skinfold caliper
Spirometer
Force plate
Goniometer alone
explanation: A force plate records the magnitude and timing of external forces applied to the ground.

subtopic: Biomechanics — movement analysis, force, kinematics
text: A laboratory wants the external vertical force during a runner's landing to be measured directly. Which instrument is most appropriate?
options: Skinfold caliper
Goniometer
Spirometer
Force plate
explanation: A force plate records ground-reaction force, including its vertical component.

subtopic: Biomechanics — movement analysis, force, kinematics
text: To compare peak landing forces on two surfaces, which measurement system provides the most direct data?
options: A force plate beneath each landing area
A body-mass index calculated before testing
A resting blood-pressure cuff during testing
A thigh-circumference tape measure at rest
explanation: Instrumented force plates directly record the ground-reaction force during landing.

subtopic: Biomechanics — movement analysis, force, kinematics
text: During a countermovement jump, which device is designed to record the athlete’s vertical ground-reaction force over time?
options: A hand-held dynamometer only
A force plate
A skinfold caliper
A pulse oximeter
explanation: A force plate measures the time-varying ground-reaction force generated against the platform.

subtopic: Biomechanics — movement analysis, force, kinematics
text: A biomechanics team needs force-time data to calculate loading rate during a landing. Which device should be selected?
options: A force plate
A stadiometer
A spirometer
A tape measure
explanation: Loading-rate calculations require force measured over time, which a force plate provides.

subtopic: Biomechanics — movement analysis, force, kinematics
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, a two-dimensional video analysis of a complex movement is limited mainly because it:
options: Directly measures joint moments from trajectories
Cannot record timing in the camera plane
Requires no calibration to estimate displacement
May miss motion outside the camera plane
explanation: A single camera view cannot fully capture out-of-plane motion or directly measure joint moments.

subtopic: Biomechanics — movement analysis, force, kinematics
text: A side-view camera records a hurdler’s sagittal motion but cannot see a lateral foot placement. What is the main limitation?
options: The camera directly measures muscle force
Motion outside the camera plane may be missed
The camera eliminates perspective error
The camera measures oxygen consumption
explanation: Two-dimensional analysis may not capture motion occurring outside the camera’s plane.

subtopic: Biomechanics — movement analysis, force, kinematics
text: A frontal video shows knee valgus during a landing. Which conclusion should be made cautiously because of the two-dimensional setup?
options: The view always measures joint torque exactly
The view proves the ACL is torn
The view may miss transverse-plane rotation
The view directly measures ground force
explanation: A 2-D view can describe projected motion but may miss out-of-plane rotation and translation.

subtopic: Biomechanics — movement analysis, force, kinematics
text: A camera aligned with the sagittal plane is used to study a cutting manoeuvre. Which feature may be under-represented?
options: Rotation and displacement outside that plane
The athlete’s body mass during the trial
The athlete’s chronological age at testing
The room’s temperature during filming
explanation: Complex cutting includes multiplanar motion that a single 2-D view may not capture.

subtopic: Biochemistry — biomarkers, metabolism, recovery indicators
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, creatine kinase after competition should be interpreted cautiously because it shows:
options: Independence from exercise type or sampling time
High individual variability and a delayed response
Direct measurement of post-exercise muscle force
A uniform response range across athletes
explanation: CK is influenced by exercise type, timing, training status, and individual biology, so one value is not diagnostic.

subtopic: Biochemistry — biomarkers, metabolism, recovery indicators
text: Two athletes record the same post-match creatine-kinase value but have very different baselines. Why should the values not be interpreted identically?
options: Creatine kinase is unrelated to muscle stress after competition
A single value always diagnoses overtraining in an athlete
Creatine kinase varies between athletes and peaks later
The marker rises only during aerobic exercise sessions
explanation: Creatine kinase varies substantially between individuals and may not peak immediately, so serial and contextual interpretation is needed.

subtopic: Biochemistry — biomarkers, metabolism, recovery indicators
text: A blood sample is taken one hour after a collision-heavy match. Why may creatine kinase not yet reflect the full response?
options: The marker may show a delayed response
The value is independent of exercise timing
The marker is produced only by the liver
The marker cannot vary between athletes
explanation: Creatine kinase responses can be delayed after muscle damage and should be interpreted with sampling time.

subtopic: Biochemistry — biomarkers, metabolism, recovery indicators
text: An athlete has high creatine kinase but little soreness the next morning. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Diagnose injury from the number alone without examination
Consider baseline, timing, symptoms, and workload
Assume the athlete has no muscle response after exercise
Ignore all subsequent measurements and symptoms
explanation: The marker has individual variability and delayed kinetics, so one value should not be interpreted in isolation.

subtopic: Biochemistry — biomarkers, metabolism, recovery indicators
text: Which monitoring plan is more defensible when using creatine kinase after repeated competition?
options: Use one universal cutoff for every athlete and test
Sample only before the first competitive season
Treat any increase as a confirmed muscle injury
Compare serial results with baseline and symptoms
explanation: Serial, individualized measurements with symptoms and workload provide more meaningful context than a single universal cutoff.

subtopic: Biochemistry — biomarkers, metabolism, recovery indicators
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, blood lactate concentration reflects the balance between production, transport, utilization, and:
options: Glycogen breakdown
Amino-acid deamination
Lactate clearance
Substrate phosphorylation
explanation: Lactate concentration reflects the net balance of its production, distribution, oxidation, and clearance.

subtopic: Biochemistry — biomarkers, metabolism, recovery indicators
text: A runner’s blood lactate is 10 mmol/L immediately after intervals. What does that value primarily represent?
options: A direct measure of exercise-related muscle damage
The athlete’s total muscle glycogen reserve
The exact oxygen content of blood and lungs
The balance of lactate production and clearance
explanation: Blood lactate concentration reflects the dynamic balance of production, transport, utilization, and clearance.

subtopic: Biochemistry — biomarkers, metabolism, recovery indicators
text: During active recovery, blood lactate falls more rapidly in one athlete than another. Which process is most directly relevant?
options: Lactate transport, utilization, and clearance
Fat storage in adipose tissue during rest
Bone remodelling during recovery from exercise
Loss of all muscle ATP during exercise
explanation: The observed concentration depends on how lactate is transported, used, and cleared as well as on production.

subtopic: Biochemistry — biomarkers, metabolism, recovery indicators
text: Two cyclists produce different lactate concentrations at the same workload. What is the soundest interpretation?
options: The higher value proves greater muscle damage
Their lactate handling processes may differ
The lower value proves no anaerobic contribution
Lactate is unrelated to exercise intensity
explanation: Lactate concentration is a net result of several simultaneous processes and should not be equated with damage alone.

subtopic: Biochemistry — biomarkers, metabolism, recovery indicators
text: When comparing post-exercise lactate between two trials, why must sampling time be standardized?
options: Lactate concentration stays fixed after exercise
Sampling time changes body height, not lactate
Lactate concentration changes during recovery
Blood volume alone determines the lactate result
explanation: Lactate kinetics continue during recovery, so timing affects the measured concentration.

subtopic: Biochemistry — biomarkers, metabolism, recovery indicators
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, ferritin is most directly related to the body's:
options: Iron stores
Joint-fluid volume
Creatine stores
Muscle glycogen stores
explanation: Ferritin is a storage protein commonly used to assess iron stores, with inflammation considered during interpretation.

subtopic: Biochemistry — biomarkers, metabolism, recovery indicators
text: An endurance athlete reports fatigue and has low ferritin. Which physiological reserve does ferritin most directly reflect?
options: Muscle glycogen
Plasma sodium
Lung volume
Iron stores
explanation: Ferritin is commonly interpreted as an indicator of stored iron, although inflammation and context also matter.

subtopic: Biochemistry — biomarkers, metabolism, recovery indicators
text: A runner has a low ferritin concentration with otherwise normal hydration. Which finding is most relevant to investigate?
options: Reduced iron stores
Increased lung compliance
Excess muscle glycogen
High body-water content
explanation: Low ferritin may indicate depleted iron stores and warrants appropriate clinical interpretation.

subtopic: Biochemistry — biomarkers, metabolism, recovery indicators
text: An athlete’s ferritin is low despite normal haemoglobin. What does the result most directly suggest?
options: The athlete has excessive plasma volume
Iron stores may be reduced before overt anaemia
The athlete has maximal aerobic capacity
The athlete’s muscle glycogen is depleted
explanation: Ferritin reflects storage iron and can be low even when haemoglobin has not yet fallen.

subtopic: Biochemistry — biomarkers, metabolism, recovery indicators
text: Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant, but in a stable athlete a low value remains most concerning for reduced:
options: Ventilatory threshold
Muscle fibre length
Iron stores
Joint range of motion
explanation: A low ferritin value is most directly associated with low stored iron, while inflammation can complicate interpretation of a normal or high value.

subtopic: Biochemistry — biomarkers, metabolism, recovery indicators
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, an elevated biomarker immediately after eccentric exercise may be misleading because:
options: The marker is unaffected by exercise intensity
The sample may precede the marker's peak response
The marker must peak immediately after exercise stops
A single measurement provides a complete diagnosis
explanation: Many exercise biomarkers have delayed kinetics, so timing and repeated context are essential.

subtopic: Biochemistry — biomarkers, metabolism, recovery indicators
text: A biomarker is measured ten minutes after an unfamiliar eccentric session. Why might the result underestimate the later response?
options: Eccentric exercise prevents all marker changes
The marker peaks before every session
Sampling time cannot affect biomarker concentration
The sample may precede the marker’s peak response
explanation: Many exercise-related biomarker responses evolve over time, so an immediate sample may precede the peak.

subtopic: Biochemistry — biomarkers, metabolism, recovery indicators
text: A sports-science team wants to describe the response to eccentric exercise. Which sampling plan is more informative than one immediate sample?
options: Collect only after the season has ended
Sample at randomly chosen times for each athlete
Use serial samples across the response period
Replace biological measures with BMI alone
explanation: Serial standardized sampling helps identify the time course and possible peak response.

subtopic: Biochemistry — biomarkers, metabolism, recovery indicators
text: An elevated value is found immediately after eccentric exercise. What is the most cautious conclusion?
options: The value may not represent the eventual peak response
The value cannot be related to exercise timing
The value proves the tissue has fully recovered
The value is identical for all athletes
explanation: Immediate post-exercise values may be misleading when the marker’s response is delayed.

subtopic: Strength & Conditioning — training principles, load, recovery
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, progressive overload means that training must eventually provide:
options: Maximal intensity in every training session
More volume without adequate recovery
A greater or new stimulus beyond adaptation
The same demand in every training session
explanation: Adaptation requires a challenging but recoverable stimulus that exceeds the athlete's current tolerance.

subtopic: Strength & Conditioning — training principles, load, recovery
text: An athlete’s performance has plateaued after months at the same workload. What does progressive overload require?
options: Removing all training stimulus from the plan
Repeating the identical workload indefinitely
Reducing every session to recovery intensity
A greater or new stimulus beyond current adaptation
explanation: Progressive overload requires a gradually greater or changed stimulus as the athlete adapts.

subtopic: Strength & Conditioning — training principles, load, recovery
text: After an athlete adapts to a resistance load, which programming change best illustrates progressive overload?
options: Increase a relevant training demand while preserving technique
Remove resistance and retain only stretching between sessions
Keep every variable identical throughout the entire block
Increase load without regard to readiness or technique
explanation: Overload is introduced by a planned increase in a relevant demand, with technique and recovery considered.

subtopic: Strength & Conditioning — training principles, load, recovery
text: Which change is the clearest example of progressive overload for a trained lifter?
options: Repeat the same load despite clear adaptation to it
Increase a tolerated 3 × 8 load slightly with sound technique
Replace all lifting with passive recovery between sessions
Add maximal load without any progression plan or testing
explanation: A planned increase in load after adaptation provides a new stimulus while retaining a safe progression.

subtopic: Strength & Conditioning — training principles, load, recovery
text: A training load that once challenged an athlete now feels easy. What is the appropriate principle for the next block?
options: Assume further adaptation is automatic
Remove sport-specific work from training
Introduce a planned new or greater stimulus
Use maximal testing every day
explanation: When adaptation reduces the challenge, a planned increase or change in stimulus is needed for further progression.

subtopic: Strength & Conditioning — training principles, load, recovery
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, training specificity means that adaptations depend strongly on the:
options: Session location without intensity details
Total weekly training time without mode
Preferred equipment without movement demands
Mode, intensity, duration, and movement demands
explanation: Adaptations are specific to the muscles, energy systems, velocities, and skills repeatedly stressed.

subtopic: Strength & Conditioning — training principles, load, recovery
text: A coach prepares a sprinter and a marathoner with the same programme. Which principle explains why their adaptations will differ?
options: Specificity reflects mode, intensity, duration, and movement
Training frequency alone determines every adaptation
All exercise produces identical adaptations in every sport
Body mass alone determines adaptation to training
explanation: Training adaptations are specific to the mode, intensity, duration, and movement pattern of the stimulus.

subtopic: Strength & Conditioning — training principles, load, recovery
text: A cyclist adds many hours of cycling but wants to improve repeated cutting in football. Which limitation should be expected?
options: Cycling automatically improves change-of-direction skill
Cycling does not reproduce football cutting demands
Training mode has no effect on adaptation
Endurance work directly measures cutting technique
explanation: Specificity means cycling adaptations do not fully reproduce the neuromuscular and movement demands of football cutting.

subtopic: Strength & Conditioning — training principles, load, recovery
text: A rehabilitation programme restores strength but omits acceleration and change-of-direction drills before soccer return. Which principle is being overlooked?
options: Strength eliminates all sport-specific requirements
Only body mass determines training transfer
Training should reflect sport movement and intensity
Recovery makes sport specificity unnecessary
explanation: Return preparation should progressively reproduce the movement, speed, and intensity demands of the sport.

subtopic: Strength & Conditioning — training principles, load, recovery
text: A rower uses heavy upper-body lifting to improve a technical rowing phase. What should guide the transfer decision?
options: Similarity to the target movement and demand
Whether the exercise causes maximal soreness
The number of exercises completed in the session
The athlete’s chronological age at testing
explanation: Specificity concerns how closely the training mode and demands resemble the performance task.

subtopic: Strength & Conditioning — training principles, load, recovery
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, training density describes the relationship between work and:
options: Total training volume accumulated weekly
Number of exercises in the program
Mean load used across the session
Recovery time between work bouts
explanation: Density reflects work performed per unit time or the rest available between work bouts.

subtopic: Strength & Conditioning — training principles, load, recovery
text: Eight 30-second intervals are performed with either 30 or 60 seconds of rest. The 30-second-rest session has greater training:
options: Volume
Density
Flexibility
Body composition
explanation: Training density increases when a similar amount of work is completed in less elapsed time or with shorter recovery.

subtopic: Strength & Conditioning — training principles, load, recovery
text: In a repeated-sprint circuit, what variable most directly describes the relationship between work bouts and the recovery interval?
options: Training density
Joint torque
Somatotype
Vital capacity
explanation: Training density describes how work is distributed relative to recovery and elapsed session time.

subtopic: Strength & Conditioning — training principles, load, recovery
text: A coach shortens rest while keeping the number of intervals and work duration unchanged. What training variable has been increased?
options: Athlete height
Muscle insertion length
Skinfold thickness
Session density
explanation: Shorter recovery raises the amount of work performed per unit of session time.

subtopic: Strength & Conditioning — training principles, load, recovery
text: Two conditioning sessions contain the same total work, but one finishes sooner because recovery is shorter. Which session has the greater:
options: Training specificity
Training density
Maximal strength
Biological maturity
explanation: The same work compressed into less time represents greater training density.

subtopic: Strength & Conditioning — training principles, load, recovery
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, a taper before an important competition usually reduces training volume while:
options: Maintaining selected intensity and sport-specific quality
Eliminating intensity while preserving unrelated volume
Maintaining the same volume and increasing fatigue
Stopping all sport-specific practice until competition
explanation: Tapering reduces fatigue while preserving fitness with selected intensity and specificity.

subtopic: Strength & Conditioning — training principles, load, recovery
text: A middle-distance runner tapers before a major race. Which change is most consistent with the principle?
options: Stop all sport-specific intensity before race day
Increase training volume until the day of racing
Replace training with repeated maximal testing
Reduce volume while retaining key intensity and quality
explanation: A taper generally reduces training volume while preserving selected intensity and sport-specific quality.

subtopic: Strength & Conditioning — training principles, load, recovery
text: A swimmer cuts weekly metres before a championship but retains short race-pace repetitions. Why is this approach used?
options: It removes useful adaptation before the championship
It guarantees a new maximal strength record in racing
It reduces fatigue while retaining race-specific quality
It increases cumulative training stress before racing
explanation: Reducing volume can dissipate fatigue while selected intensity preserves sport-specific readiness.

subtopic: Strength & Conditioning — training principles, load, recovery
text: During the final week before competition, which taper decision is most defensible?
options: Increase every session’s volume before competition
Lower volume while retaining selected high-quality efforts
Add unfamiliar exercises to create soreness before racing
Eliminate all intensity and movement practice
explanation: Maintaining selected quality while reducing volume supports readiness without unnecessarily adding fatigue.

subtopic: Psychology — motivation, stress, arousal, mental readiness
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, intrinsic motivation is characterized by participation driven primarily by:
options: Interest and enjoyment from the activity itself
Avoidance of criticism or punishment from others
Recognition and rewards provided by others
Pressure to meet an externally imposed standard
explanation: Intrinsic motivation arises from inherent interest, enjoyment, or satisfaction in the activity.

subtopic: Psychology — motivation, stress, arousal, mental readiness
text: A runner continues training when no prize is offered because the activity itself is satisfying. This is an example of:
options: External regulation
Amotivation
Intrinsic motivation
Avoidance conditioning
explanation: Intrinsic motivation is driven by interest, enjoyment, or satisfaction inherent in the activity.

subtopic: Psychology — motivation, stress, arousal, mental readiness
text: An athlete chooses a difficult technical drill because mastering it is enjoyable, even without coach praise. What primarily motivates the choice?
options: A financial incentive
Fear of punishment
A required attendance rule
Intrinsic motivation
explanation: Enjoyment and interest in the activity itself are characteristic of intrinsic motivation.

subtopic: Psychology — motivation, stress, arousal, mental readiness
text: A scholarship is removed, but an athlete keeps practising because learning the skill is personally rewarding. Which construct best explains this behaviour?
options: External pressure only
Avoidance of exercise
Intrinsic motivation
A loss of self-efficacy
explanation: Persistence for the inherent satisfaction of learning reflects intrinsic motivation.

subtopic: Psychology — motivation, stress, arousal, mental readiness
text: A coach wants to support intrinsic motivation during a difficult training block. Which athlete response would be the clearest indicator?
options: The athlete participates only to avoid a fine
The athlete enjoys the challenge itself
The athlete trains only when a reward is displayed
The athlete refuses all coaching feedback
explanation: Intrinsic motivation is reflected by engagement for the inherent interest or enjoyment of the activity.

subtopic: Psychology — motivation, stress, arousal, mental readiness
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, self-efficacy refers to an athlete's belief that they can:
options: Perform the actions required for a specific task
Predict an opponent's decisions accurately
Eliminate competitive pressure before every event
Control every external outcome during competition
explanation: Self-efficacy is task- and context-specific confidence in one's ability to execute behavior.

subtopic: Psychology — motivation, stress, arousal, mental readiness
text: Before a specific vault, a gymnast believes she can execute the required sequence under competition conditions. This belief is self-efficacy for:
options: Every possible sport
That specific task
The final competition result only
The coach’s performance
explanation: Self-efficacy is a task- and situation-specific belief in one’s capability to perform the required action.

subtopic: Psychology — motivation, stress, arousal, mental readiness
text: An athlete’s confidence improves after completing progressively harder successful repetitions. Which psychological mechanism is most directly involved?
options: Random fatigue eliminates self-efficacy in competition
Body mass determines self-efficacy in every task
External rewards define every belief about ability
Mastery experiences can strengthen self-efficacy
explanation: Successful mastery experiences are a major source of self-efficacy information.

subtopic: Psychology — motivation, stress, arousal, mental readiness
text: An athlete believes she can perform a penalty kick but is unsure whether the team will win. Which distinction is correct?
options: The first concerns action capability; the second, outcome
The first is somatic anxiety; the second is flexibility
The first is body image; the second is motivation
Both beliefs are identical performance measures
explanation: Self-efficacy concerns capability to perform an action, whereas outcome expectation concerns the consequence of that action.

subtopic: Psychology — motivation, stress, arousal, mental readiness
text: Which interview question best assesses sport-specific self-efficacy?
options: How tall are you compared with teammates in this squad?
How much do you enjoy every activity in daily life?
How capable do you feel of completing the final sprint?
What was the team’s final score in the last season?
explanation: A self-efficacy question asks about perceived capability for a defined task in a defined context.

subtopic: Psychology — motivation, stress, arousal, mental readiness
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, cognitive anxiety primarily involves:
options: Physiological activation such as sweating and tension
Worry and negative thoughts about performance
Belief in one's ability to execute the task
Motivation to participate in the activity
explanation: Cognitive anxiety concerns worry and apprehension, whereas somatic anxiety concerns perceived physiological symptoms.

subtopic: Psychology — motivation, stress, arousal, mental readiness
text: Before a final, a gymnast repeatedly imagines falling and worries about being judged. Which component of anxiety is most evident?
options: Somatic recovery
Muscular hypertrophy
Intrinsic motivation
Cognitive anxiety
explanation: Cognitive anxiety involves worry, negative thoughts, and concerns about performance consequences.

subtopic: Psychology — motivation, stress, arousal, mental readiness
text: Which response is primarily cognitive rather than somatic anxiety before a race?
options: Worry that a mistake will confirm poor ability
Sweaty palms before the race begins
Tight abdominal muscles under competitive pressure
A rapid heartbeat during the start of competition
explanation: Worry and negative performance thoughts are cognitive symptoms; autonomic and muscular sensations are somatic symptoms.

subtopic: Psychology — motivation, stress, arousal, mental readiness
text: An athlete reports persistent thoughts about failing the selection trial but no unusual muscle tension. Which state is most consistent with:
options: Somatic anxiety only
Delayed muscle soreness
Cognitive anxiety
Training specificity
explanation: The defining feature described is performance-related worry and negative thought content.

subtopic: Psychology — motivation, stress, arousal, mental readiness
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, a pre-performance routine is useful because it can provide:
options: Consistent attentional cues before performance
A substitute for technical practice
Prevention of every physiological stress response
A guaranteed outcome independent of execution
explanation: A routine organizes controllable preparation and attention without guaranteeing an outcome.

subtopic: Psychology — motivation, stress, arousal, mental readiness
text: A tennis player uses the same breath, visual target, and racquet cue before every serve. What is the likely function of this routine?
options: Guarantee a successful competitive outcome
Replace all technical practice before the event
Increase random distraction during preparation
Provide consistent attentional cues before performance
explanation: A pre-performance routine can organize attention and create consistent cues without guaranteeing the outcome.

subtopic: Psychology — motivation, stress, arousal, mental readiness
text: A basketball player follows the same dribble-breathe-look sequence before a free throw. Why may this routine help?
options: It makes the shot independent of technical skill
It removes the need for a physical warm-up
It creates repeatable attentional and behavioural cues
It ensures the opponent cannot defend the shot
explanation: Consistent routines can help focus attention and regulate preparation before a skill.

subtopic: Psychology — motivation, stress, arousal, mental readiness
text: After a missed penalty, a footballer returns to a brief breath-and-focus sequence before the next attempt. Which purpose is most defensible?
options: Erase the previous result from the scoreboard
Reset attention with a consistent cue
Avoid all performance feedback after the error
Guarantee the next kick will score
explanation: A routine can help redirect attention to controllable preparation after an error.

subtopic: Nutrition — macronutrients, hydration, energy balance
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, carbohydrate availability is especially important during high-intensity exercise because carbohydrate supports:
options: Primary use of protein as immediate fuel
Primary reliance on fat oxidation during maximal work
Rapid ATP production and muscle glycogen use
Long-term bone remodeling during the exercise bout
explanation: High-intensity work relies heavily on glycolytic and glycogen-derived carbohydrate metabolism.

subtopic: Nutrition — macronutrients, hydration, energy balance
text: A midfielder must repeat high-intensity sprints late in a match. Why is carbohydrate availability especially relevant?
options: It prevents all fluid loss during intense exercise
It replaces the need for oxygen during the match
It supplies no usable energy during exercise
It supports rapid ATP production and muscle glycogen use
explanation: Carbohydrate supports high-rate ATP production and contributes to muscle-glycogen use during intense intermittent exercise.

subtopic: Nutrition — macronutrients, hydration, energy balance
text: A footballer fades during repeated high-intensity runs after beginning the match with low glycogen. Which role of carbohydrate is most relevant?
options: Supporting rapid ATP production from muscle glycogen
Reducing all sweat production during exercise
Replacing neuromuscular coordination in sprinting
Providing only structural protein for recovery
explanation: High-intensity intermittent work relies substantially on carbohydrate availability and muscle glycogen.

subtopic: Nutrition — macronutrients, hydration, energy balance
text: During repeated intervals above race pace, which fuel contribution is most directly supported by adequate carbohydrate availability?
options: Exclusive oxidation of stored fat during intervals
Rapid ATP production and muscle glycogen use
Elimination of oxygen demand during sprinting
Immediate bone mineralization after exercise
explanation: Carbohydrate can provide ATP rapidly and supports glycogen-dependent high-intensity work.

subtopic: Nutrition — macronutrients, hydration, energy balance
text: An athlete has two hard sessions in one day. Which nutrition priority helps preserve high-intensity capacity in the second session?
options: Avoid all carbohydrate after the first hard session
Use passive stretching instead of carbohydrate
Replace carbohydrate to replenish glycogen between sessions
Consume fluid without considering total energy needs
explanation: Restoring carbohydrate availability helps replenish glycogen needed for subsequent high-intensity exercise.

subtopic: Nutrition — macronutrients, hydration, energy balance
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, a body-mass loss of about two percent during exercise most strongly suggests:
options: Reduced glycogen stores without associated water loss
Increased lean tissue during the exercise bout
Acute fat loss as the primary explanation for change
Meaningful fluid loss that raises physiological strain
explanation: Rapid exercise-associated mass loss is primarily fluid loss and can impair thermoregulation and performance.

subtopic: Nutrition — macronutrients, hydration, energy balance
text: A 70-kg runner finishes a hot session 1.4 kg lighter. What does this change most strongly suggest?
options: A 2% gain in lean mass during the session
Meaningful fluid loss that can increase strain
A measure of aerobic capacity from body mass alone
A complete loss of body fat during the run
explanation: A 1.4-kg loss from 70 kg is 2% of body mass and is consistent with substantial fluid loss during exercise.

subtopic: Nutrition — macronutrients, hydration, energy balance
text: During a humid tournament, an athlete finishes 2.1% below pre-session body mass. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: The athlete likely has meaningful fluid loss
The change directly measures glycogen synthesis
The change proves a bone injury occurred
The athlete has gained lean tissue during exercise
explanation: A body-mass reduction of about 2% during exercise commonly indicates substantial net fluid loss and increased strain.

subtopic: Nutrition — macronutrients, hydration, energy balance
text: A practitioner compares pre- and post-exercise body mass after a long run. Why is a fall of about 2% clinically relevant?
options: It proves that all lost mass was body fat
It is too small to interpret in every setting
It directly measures blood lactate concentration
It suggests fluid loss that can increase strain
explanation: A 2% exercise-related mass loss is a useful indicator of meaningful fluid deficit, with context considered.

subtopic: Nutrition — macronutrients, hydration, energy balance
text: An athlete begins a match at 75 kg and ends at 73.5 kg without replacing fluids. What is the approximate percentage loss and its likely meaning?
options: 0.2%; increased muscle mass
2%; meaningful fluid loss
20%; normal measurement error
5%; improved hydration
explanation: The 1.5-kg loss is 2% of 75 kg and most plausibly reflects meaningful fluid loss during the match.

subtopic: Nutrition — macronutrients, hydration, energy balance
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, low energy availability may increase an athlete's risk of impaired:
options: Health, recovery, endocrine function, and performance
Performance without broader physiological effects
Bone health while protecting endocrine and immune function
Immune function only when training load is light
explanation: Low energy availability can affect endocrine, bone, immune, metabolic, and performance outcomes.

subtopic: Nutrition — macronutrients, hydration, energy balance
text: An athlete combines high training volume with chronically inadequate intake. Which group of outcomes may be impaired by low energy availability?
options: Only height and arm span during adolescent growth
Only acute heart rate after strenuous exercise
Only short-term motivation during training
Health, recovery, endocrine function, and performance
explanation: Low energy availability can affect multiple physiological systems, recovery, health, and performance.

subtopic: Nutrition — macronutrients, hydration, energy balance
text: A distance runner has persistent fatigue, menstrual disturbances, and recurrent bone stress symptoms while restricting intake. Which broader risk pattern is concerning?
options: Improved recovery without any health consequence for the athlete
Impaired health, recovery, endocrine function, and performance
A change limited to hydration status during training
A purely technical skill deficit during sport performance
explanation: Low energy availability can disrupt endocrine and bone health while impairing recovery and performance.

subtopic: Nutrition — macronutrients, hydration, energy balance
text: A coach observes declining performance and poor recovery during aggressive weight reduction. Which consequence should be considered?
options: Low energy availability can impair health and performance
Weight reduction always improves adaptation and recovery
Only sprint technique is affected by energy intake
Energy availability has no relationship with recovery
explanation: Insufficient energy relative to exercise expenditure can impair health, recovery, endocrine function, and performance.

subtopic: Nutrition — macronutrients, hydration, energy balance
text: For an athlete entering a new training block, a supplement used by an athlete should be evaluated for evidence, dose, contamination risk, and:
options: Marketing claims and number of ingredients
Cost compared with similar products on the market
Its status under applicable anti-doping rules
Whether teammates commonly use the same product
explanation: Supplement decisions require evidence appraisal, safety checks, contamination awareness, and anti-doping review.

subtopic: Nutrition — macronutrients, hydration, energy balance
text: Before recommending a supplement to an athlete, which additional check is essential after reviewing evidence, dose, and contamination risk?
options: Its colour and package size on the label
Its status under applicable anti-doping rules
Whether it guarantees selection for competition
Whether it replaces all meals during training
explanation: Supplement decisions should include evidence, dose, contamination risk, and applicable anti-doping status.

subtopic: Nutrition — macronutrients, hydration, energy balance
text: A product has plausible ingredients and third-party testing, but the athlete competes under anti-doping rules. What must still be checked?
options: Whether the label promises a personal best
Whether it can replace sleep during a training block
Whether its container is the largest available size
Whether its ingredients comply with anti-doping rules
explanation: Third-party testing reduces but does not eliminate the need to review ingredients and anti-doping status.

subtopic: Nutrition — macronutrients, hydration, energy balance
text: An athlete wants to start a supplement immediately before an international event. Which decision process is most defensible?
options: Use it because a teammate recommends the product
Assume a natural product is automatically permitted
Check evidence, dose, contamination, and anti-doping status
Ignore the label when the recommended dose is small
explanation: A risk-based supplement decision requires evidence appraisal and checking contamination and anti-doping implications.
